title: In everything give thanks (1 Thessalonians 5:18)

segments.voice: Yesterday, spiritual friendship: Aelred and the third one in the room. Your line was friendship is holy. Did your thank-you go out, and what came back? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-four.

"Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks." Three short lines near the end of Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians. On a coffee mug they'd look cheerful, almost easy. Then read the letter around them. Paul says this church received the word "in much affliction." He writes to comfort them about friends who have died, those he calls "them which are asleep." These are people in trouble and in grief. And to them, not to people having a good week, he writes: in every thing, give thanks. Today, gratitude as a daily practice.

Look at the small word in the middle. The King James reads: "In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you." In every thing. Some readers lean hard on that little word. On their reading, Paul doesn't ask the grieving to be thankful that their friends died. He asks them to find thanks inside whatever is happening. Other readers point to Ephesians, which says "giving thanks always for all things," and hold the two lines together. Either way, the thanks doesn't wait for the trouble to clear. Paul seems to have practiced it himself. Writing to the Philippians while in bonds, he says: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content." Learned. Something practiced, not something he was born with. And there's an older pattern behind him. Psalm 136 repeats one refrain, line after line: "for his mercy endureth for ever." Thanks as a rhythm, said again and again until it sinks in. Then one more example. On the night Jesus was betrayed, Luke says, "he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it." Thanks, at that table, on that night. Christians build this into ordinary days. A grace said before a meal. A few minutes at bedtime looking back for the day's gifts. A line of thanks at the start of prayer, before any asking. Not a feeling summoned on command. A habit of looking.

Here's the practice: list ten gifts. Settle, and breathe. Count them on your fingers, one at a time, and keep them small and specific. Not my family, but the way your sister laughed on the phone. Not health, but the knee that worked on the stairs this morning. Hot water. A song. A text that came at the right moment. If the day has been hard, look inside it anyway, the way Paul asked. If you run out before ten, wait a breath and look again. If you pray, you can say thanks for each one. The bell holds the time.
In everything give thanks. Paul's line to a grieving church: thanks found inside every situation, not saved for the good days.
Your line: in everything, thanks. Today, before one meal, stop for a breath and name one thing you're grateful for, even on a hard day. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Christians practice gratitude through grace before meals, thanksgiving at the start of prayer, and some through a nightly review of the day's gifts; churches give thanks in worship together, and some keep special days of thanksgiving.

fork.setup: you're in the church at Thessalonica. you've buried friends and faced trouble. a letter from Paul is read aloud. what does it ask of you?
options: wait until things get better, then give thanks.
give thanks only for the good parts, and ignore the rest.
fork.reveal: "rejoice evermore. pray without ceasing. in every thing give thanks." written to people in grief, not to people having a good week.

original.note: Greek, 1 Thessalonians 5:18: give thanks — a command, addressed to the whole church.

notes: The 'in' vs 'for' distinction is attributed to 'some readers' and balanced with Ephesians 5:20; confirm fair.
'Writing to the Philippians while in bonds' rests on Philippians 1:13 ('my bonds in Christ'); the place of imprisonment is left unstated on purpose.
Psalm 136: 'repeats one refrain, line after line' — the refrain closes each verse in the KJV; confirm wording.
Trapdoor: εὐχαριστεῖτε read as a present imperative ('keep on giving thanks'); confirm the gloss is not overpressed.
Index word 'In everything give thanks' differs from the KJV spelling 'In every thing'; quotations keep the KJV.
